rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: An equiconvex lens of focal length 15 cm is cut into two equal plano-convex halves. The focal length of each half will be :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (A): 30 cm.**

**The cut is what the question is about**, so identify it first. Cutting an equiconvex lens into two **plano-convex** halves means slicing **perpendicular to the principal axis** — through the middle, parallel to the flat faces that result. Each half keeps **one** curved surface and gains a flat one.

**The original lens.** Equiconvex means \(R_1 = +R\) and \(R_2 = -R\), so by the lensmaker's formula

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \left(n-1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{-R}\right) = \left(n-1\right)\dfrac{2}{R}\)

\(\dfrac{1}{15} = \dfrac{2\left(n-1\right)}{R}\)

**Each half.** One curved surface of radius \(R\), one plane surface \(\left(R \to \infty\right)\):

\(\dfrac{1}{f'} = \left(n-1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{\infty}\right) = \dfrac{\left(n-1\right)}{R}\)

**That is exactly HALF of \(1/f\)**, so

\(\dfrac{1}{f'} = \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{15} = \dfrac{1}{30}\)

\(\boxed{\ f' = 30\ \mathrm{cm}\ }\)

**Losing one curved surface halves the POWER, and so doubles the focal length.** Each surface contributes equally to the bending, and removing one leaves half the converging power behind.

**Option (C), 15 cm, is the answer for the OTHER cut**, and it is there on purpose. Slicing the lens **along** the principal axis — into two semicircular halves — leaves both curved surfaces intact on each piece. The radii are unchanged, so the focal length is unchanged at \(15\) cm; only the aperture is halved, which dims the image without moving it.

**So "cut into two equal halves" is ambiguous until the word plano-convex settles it.** The shape of the pieces tells you which cut was made, and the two cuts give different answers.

**In terms of power**, which is the cleaner statement:

\(P_{\text{original}} = P_{\text{surface 1}} + P_{\text{surface 2}} = 2P_{\text{surface}}\)

so one surface alone gives \(P/2\) and \(f' = 2f\).

**Recombining the two halves** face to face reproduces the original: \(1/F = 1/30 + 1/30 = 1/15\), giving \(F = 15\) cm \(\checkmark\). That check is worth doing, because it confirms the halving rather than assuming it.

**A note on what does not change.** The refractive index and the radius of curvature belong to the glass and the grinding; cutting alters neither. Only the **number of refracting surfaces** changes, and the focal length follows.

rows.subtopic: Electric Dipole and Dipole in a Uniform Field
rows.stem: An electric dipole \(\vec{P} = 2qa\,\hat{i}\) is placed in x-y plane, centred at the origin. Let \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) be the magnitudes of electric field at a point distant r (>> a) from its centre, along its axis and on its equatorial plane, respectively. Then the value of \(\left(\dfrac{E_1}{E_2}\right)\) is :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (C): 2.**

**The two standard dipole fields**, both for \(r \gg a\):

**Along the AXIS** (the end-on position, in line with \(\vec{p}\)):

\(E_1 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{2p}{r^{3}}\)

**On the EQUATORIAL plane** (the broadside position, perpendicular to \(\vec{p}\) through its centre):

\(E_2 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{p}{r^{3}}\)

**The ratio:**

\(\dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = \dfrac{2p/r^{3}}{p/r^{3}}\)

\(\boxed{\ \dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = 2\ }\)

**Everything cancels except the factor of 2** — the dipole moment, the distance, the constants. The ratio is **universal**, the same for every dipole at every distance in the far field.

**Why the axial field is the stronger one.** On the axis, the near charge is closer than the far charge, so their fields differ in magnitude and point in **opposite** directions; the difference survives and points along \(\vec{p}\). On the equatorial plane both charges are **equidistant**, their fields have equal magnitude, and the components along \(\vec{p}\) cancel while the perpendicular components add — leaving a field **antiparallel** to \(\vec{p}\), and smaller.

**So the two fields differ in DIRECTION as well as magnitude**, though the question asks only for the ratio of magnitudes. Axial field parallel to \(\vec{p}\), equatorial field antiparallel to it.

**Both fall off as \(1/r^{3}\)**, not \(1/r^{2}\). That steeper decay is the signature of a dipole: the two charges are equal and opposite, so their monopole fields cancel at large distance and what remains is the residue of their separation. This is why a neutral molecule's field dies away so much faster than an ion's.

**Where \(r \gg a\) is needed.** The exact axial field is

\(E_1 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{2pr}{\left(r^{2}-a^{2}\right)^{2}}\)

which reduces to \(2p/4\pi\varepsilon_0r^{3}\) only when \(a\) is negligible beside \(r\). Closer in, the ratio is **not** exactly \(2\), and the whole dipole approximation breaks down.

**A note on the orientation given.** The dipole \(\vec{p} = 2qa\,\hat{i}\) lies along \(x\), so "along its axis" means on the \(x\)-axis and "on its equatorial plane" means in the \(yz\)-plane through the origin. That geometry does not enter the ratio, which is why the result is a bare number.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: A plano-convex lens, made of glass (n = \(1{\cdot}5\)) has a curved surface whose radius is 40 cm. The image formed of an object is of the same size as that of the object. The distance of the object from the lens is :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (C): 160 cm.**

**Two steps: find the focal length, then use the magnification condition.**

**Step 1 — the focal length.** For a plano-convex lens, one surface has radius \(R\) and the other is flat \(\left(R \to \infty\right)\):

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \left(n-1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{\infty}\right) = \dfrac{n-1}{R}\)

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}5 - 1}{40} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}5}{40} = \dfrac{1}{80}\)

\(f = 80\ \mathrm{cm}\)

**Step 2 — where the image is the same size as the object.** For a converging lens, \(\left|m\right| = 1\) with a **real** image occurs at one place only:

\(u = 2f\)

\(\boxed{\ \text{object distance} = 2 \times 80 = 160\ \mathrm{cm}\ }\)

*Confirming with the lens equation:* with \(u = -160\) and \(f = +80\),

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{80} + \dfrac{1}{-160} = \dfrac{2-1}{160} = \dfrac{1}{160}\)

so \(v = +160\) cm and \(m = -v/u = -160/\left(-160\right)\cdot\left(-1\right) = -1\) — same size, **inverted**, real \(\checkmark\).

**Option (B), 80 cm, is the focal length itself**, and it is the trap: an object at \(f\) produces an image at **infinity**, not one of equal size. Stopping after step 1 lands exactly on it.

**Why \(2f\) is the unique real-image solution.** Writing \(m = f/\left(f - u_{\text{signed}}\right)\), the magnitude is \(1\) only when the object is at \(2f\) (image real and inverted) or at the lens itself (trivial). **A virtual image of a converging lens is always magnified**, never the same size, so no second answer exists on that side.

**\(u = v = 2f\) is a symmetric configuration**, and it is the minimum possible object-to-image distance for a real image with a converging lens — \(4f = 320\) cm here. Any other real-image arrangement puts them further apart. That fact is the basis of the **displacement method** for measuring focal length, in which the lens is moved between two positions that both give sharp images.

**A note on which face is curved.** The answer does not depend on it. Turning the lens round swaps a plane surface for a curved one and vice versa, and the lensmaker's formula gives the same \(f\) either way — a general property of thin lenses. Only the aberrations differ.

**The sign convention, briefly.** Distances are measured from the optical centre with light travelling left to right; the object distance is negative and a real image distance positive. Working with magnitudes and quoting the final answer as a distance, as above, avoids most sign errors — provided the lens equation itself is applied with signs intact.

rows.stem: A metallic rod of 1 m length is rotated with a frequency of 40 rev/s, with one end hinged at the centre and the other end at the circumference of a circular metallic ring of radius 1 m, about an axis passing through the centre and perpendicular to the plane of the ring. A constant and uniform magnetic field of \(0{\cdot}5\) T parallel to the axis is present in the region. The value of emf induced between the centre and the metallic ring is close to :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (D): 63 V.**

**A rod rotating in a magnetic field** generates a motional emf between its ends:

\(\varepsilon = \dfrac{1}{2}B\omega l^{2}\)

**Where the formula comes from.** Each element \(dx\) at distance \(x\) from the hinge moves at speed \(v = \omega x\), and contributes \(dV = Bv\,dx = B\omega x\,dx\). Integrating from \(0\) to \(l\):

\(\varepsilon = \int_{0}^{l}B\omega x\,dx = \dfrac{1}{2}B\omega l^{2}\)

**The factor \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) is the integration**, not a convention — the rod's tip moves fast while the hinged end is stationary, so the average speed is half the tip speed.

**Convert the frequency to ANGULAR frequency:**

\(\omega = 2\pi\nu = 2\pi\times 40 = 251{\cdot}3\ \mathrm{rad/s}\)

**Substituting:**

\(\varepsilon = \dfrac{1}{2}\times 0{\cdot}5 \times 251{\cdot}3 \times \left(1\right)^{2}\)

\(\boxed{\ \varepsilon = 62{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{V} \approx 63\ \mathrm{V}\ }\)

**A compact form** worth noting, since the \(2\pi\) and the \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) partly cancel:

\(\varepsilon = \dfrac{1}{2}B\left(2\pi\nu\right)l^{2} = \pi\nu Bl^{2} = \pi\times 40\times 0{\cdot}5\times 1 = 62{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{V}\)

**The two ways to go wrong both involve the \(2\pi\).** Using \(\nu = 40\) in place of \(\omega\) gives \(10\) V; omitting the \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) gives \(126\) V. Revolutions per second must become radians per second before the formula is used.

**What the ring is for.** It completes the circuit so that the emf can be measured — a sliding contact runs on it while the hinge contacts the centre. **The ring itself generates nothing**: it is stationary, so no part of it cuts field lines. The emf is entirely the rod's.

**An equivalent view, by flux.** In time \(t\) the rod sweeps a sector of area \(\tfrac{1}{2}l^{2}\omega t\), so the flux it sweeps changes at the rate \(B\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}l^{2}\omega\) — the same expression. Faraday's law and the motional-emf integral agree, as they must.

**The emf is STEADY, not alternating.** The rod sweeps area at a constant rate whatever its angular position, so this arrangement is a **direct**-current generator — a homopolar or Faraday disc, the earliest form of electrical generator. An ordinary alternator differs by having the loop **rotate within** the field rather than sweep around an axis parallel to it.

**Note that \(l\) and the ring radius are both \(1\) m**, so the rod exactly spans from centre to rim. The ring's radius plays no part in the formula; only the rod's length does.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: Which of the following p-n junction diodes is forward biased ?

options.label: A
options.text: a diode between a left terminal at \(+5\) V and a right terminal at \(+10\) V

options.label: B
options.text: a diode between a left terminal at \(-1{\cdot}0\) V and a right terminal at \(-1{\cdot}5\) V

options.label: C
options.text: a diode between a left terminal at 0 V and a right terminal at 1 V

options.label: D
options.text: a diode between a left terminal at \(-2\) V and a right terminal at 0 V

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - all four options are drawn circuits. Each shows a single diode symbol connected between two open terminals whose potentials are printed beside them; those printed potentials are the only part reproduced in the option text above. WITHHELD deliberately: the ORIENTATION of the diode symbol in each option (which way the triangle and its bar face), because that, together with the two potentials, is exactly what the question tests. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
**The answer is (B).**

**Read the diode symbols first.** In all four options the triangle points to the **right**, with the bar on the right — so in every case the **p-side (anode) is the LEFT terminal** and the n-side (cathode) is the right one. That uniformity is what makes the question a straight comparison of two numbers.

**A diode is forward biased when its p-side is at the HIGHER potential:**

\(V_{\text{left}} > V_{\text{right}}\)

**Testing each option:**

| | Left | Right | \(V_L - V_R\) | Bias |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | \(+5\) V | \(+10\) V | \(-5\) V | reverse |
| **(B)** | \(-1{\cdot}0\) V | \(-1{\cdot}5\) V | \(+0{\cdot}5\) V | **forward** |
| (C) | \(0\) V | \(1\) V | \(-1\) V | reverse |
| (D) | \(-2\) V | \(0\) V | \(-2\) V | reverse |

\(\boxed{\ \text{(B) is forward biased, by } 0{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{V}\ }\)

**Option (B) is the one with BOTH terminals negative, and that is exactly the trap.** "Negative voltage must mean reverse bias" is a natural but wrong reading. **Only the DIFFERENCE across the diode matters**, never the absolute values — \(-1{\cdot}0\) V is higher than \(-1{\cdot}5\) V, so the p-side is the more positive of the two and the diode conducts.

**The same point from the opposite side.** In option (A) both terminals are strongly positive, yet the diode is reverse biased by \(5\) V, because the n-side is the higher one. Sign of the individual potentials tells you nothing; only their order does.

**Why potential DIFFERENCE is the physical quantity.** The zero of potential is a matter of where the earth symbol is drawn, and shifting every node by a constant changes no current anywhere. **A diode responds to the field across its junction**, which depends on the difference and nothing else. Adding \(2\) V to every terminal in the table would leave every entry in the last column unchanged.

**A caveat about (B) in practice.** A forward bias of \(0{\cdot}5\) V is **below the knee voltage** of a silicon diode, which is about \(0{\cdot}7\) V. So the diode is genuinely forward biased — the question's term — but would pass only a small current; it is not yet conducting freely. For germanium, whose knee is near \(0{\cdot}3\) V, it would conduct properly. The question asks about the bias, not the current.

**What forward bias does at the junction.** The applied field opposes the built-in field, **narrowing the depletion region** and lowering the potential barrier, so majority carriers can diffuse across in quantity. Reverse bias does the opposite — it widens the depletion region and raises the barrier, leaving only the tiny reverse saturation current.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: The velocity of the photoelectrons emitted from a surface depends upon the :

options.label: C
options.text: Work function of the surface only

options.label: D
options.text: Both wavelength of the incident radiation and work function of the surface

rows.solution:
**The answer is (D): both the wavelength of the incident radiation and the work function of the surface.**

**Einstein's photoelectric equation** gives the maximum kinetic energy, and hence the maximum velocity:

\(\dfrac{1}{2}mv_{\max}^{2} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \phi_0\)

\(v_{\max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{m}\left(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \phi_0\right)}\)

**Two quantities appear on the right, and both belong to the answer:**

- \(\lambda\) — the **wavelength of the incident light**, which fixes the energy \(hc/\lambda\) delivered by each photon
- \(\phi_0\) — the **work function of the surface**, the minimum energy needed to free an electron from it

**Neither alone is enough**, which rules out (A) and (C). The same light on two different metals gives different photoelectron speeds, and the same metal under two different wavelengths does too. It is the **difference** between what the photon brings and what the surface demands that appears as kinetic energy.

**Option (B), intensity, is the significant distractor, and it is the wrong answer for an important reason.** Intensity fixes the **number** of photons arriving each second, not the energy of any one of them. A photon is absorbed **whole** by a single electron and cannot be supplemented by its neighbours, so doubling the intensity doubles how many electrons are emitted while leaving each one's energy exactly as it was.

\(\text{intensity}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{photocurrent}; \qquad \text{frequency}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{kinetic energy}\)

**That separation is the whole content of the photoelectric effect**, and it is what the wave picture could not explain: a more intense wave has a larger field amplitude and ought to shake electrons free with more energy. It does not.

**The threshold, which also follows from the two named quantities.** Emission occurs only while \(hc/\lambda > \phi_0\), that is for

\(\lambda < \lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\phi_0}\)

Beyond the threshold wavelength nothing is emitted however intense the beam — another observation intensity cannot account for.

**A note on "the velocity".** Strictly the equation gives \(v_{\max}\). Emitted electrons have a **range** of speeds from zero up to that maximum, because an electron deeper inside the metal loses energy on its way out; only one from the surface, losing exactly \(\phi_0\), emerges with the full amount. The maximum is what the stopping potential measures, and what the equation predicts.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.stem: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of a neutron having kinetic energy of 150 eV.
rows.solution:
**The de Broglie wavelength from kinetic energy:**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}\)

**Step 1 — convert the energy to joules.**

\(K = 150\ \mathrm{eV} = 150 \times 1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-19} = 2{\cdot}4\times 10^{-17}\ \mathrm{J}\)

**Step 2 — the momentum.** With the neutron mass \(m_n = 1{\cdot}675\times 10^{-27}\) kg:

\(2mK = 2\left(1{\cdot}675\times 10^{-27}\right)\left(2{\cdot}4\times 10^{-17}\right) = 8{\cdot}04\times 10^{-44}\)

\(p = \sqrt{8{\cdot}04\times 10^{-44}} = 2{\cdot}84\times 10^{-22}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\)

**Step 3 — the wavelength.**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63\times 10^{-34}}{2{\cdot}84\times 10^{-22}}\)

\(\boxed{\ \lambda = 2{\cdot}33\times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m} \approx 2{\cdot}3\ \mathrm{pm}\ }\)

*The marking scheme's arithmetic substitutes \(1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-27}\) kg for the neutron and would give \(2{\cdot}4\) pm; its stated \(2{\cdot}3\) pm is the value the accurate mass produces, as above. The difference is immaterial to the physics.*

**Halving the exponent is the step to watch.** \(2mK\) is of order \(10^{-44}\), and its square root is \(10^{-22}\) — not \(10^{-44}\) again. Taking the root before dividing, rather than after, is where this calculation is usually lost.

**How small is \(2{\cdot}3\) pm?** It is about **one fortieth of an atomic diameter**, and comparable to the spacing between planes in a crystal. A neutron of this energy therefore **diffracts** from crystals, which is the basis of neutron diffraction as a structural technique.

**Why neutrons rather than electrons or X-rays.** Neutrons are **uncharged**, so they pass deep into a sample without being deflected by the electron clouds; they scatter from the **nuclei** instead. That makes them uniquely good at locating **light atoms** — hydrogen especially — which X-rays, scattering from electrons, barely see. They also carry a magnetic moment, so they reveal magnetic ordering.

**Compare the same energy given to an electron.** At \(150\) eV an electron has \(\lambda = 1{\cdot}0\) angstrom \(\left(100\ \mathrm{pm}\right)\) — some forty times longer, because \(\lambda \propto 1/\sqrt{m}\) and the neutron is about \(1840\) times heavier, giving \(\sqrt{1840} \approx 43\).

**A remark on thermal neutrons.** Neutrons in equilibrium at room temperature have \(K \approx 0{\cdot}025\) eV and \(\lambda \approx 1{\cdot}8\) angstrom — even better matched to crystal spacings, which is why reactor-based diffraction uses thermal rather than \(150\) eV neutrons. The \(1/\sqrt{K}\) dependence means the slower neutron has the longer wave.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: Explain, with the help of suitable diagram, the two important processes that occur during the formation of a p-n junction.
rows.solution:
**Two processes occur as a p-n junction forms: DIFFUSION and DRIFT.** They act in opposite directions, and the junction settles when they balance.

*To draw it:* a rectangle divided into a **p-region** on the left and an **n-region** on the right. Between them mark a narrow **depletion region** containing **negative immobile ions on the p-side** and **positive immobile ions on the n-side**. Draw arrows: **hole diffusion** and **electron diffusion** crossing the junction (p to n and n to p respectively), and **hole drift** and **electron drift** pointing the opposite way. Mark the built-in field \(\vec{E}\) pointing from the n-side to the p-side.

**1. DIFFUSION — driven by the concentration gradient.**

The p-region has a large concentration of **holes**, the n-region a large concentration of **electrons**. Across the junction those gradients are enormous, so carriers diffuse:

- **holes** diffuse from the **p-side to the n-side**
- **electrons** diffuse from the **n-side to the p-side**

**This is a flow of MAJORITY carriers**, and it constitutes the **diffusion current**, conventionally directed from p to n.

**What diffusion leaves behind.** A hole leaving the p-side exposes a fixed **negative acceptor ion**; an electron leaving the n-side exposes a fixed **positive donor ion**. These ions are locked in the crystal lattice and cannot move. The result is a thin layer near the junction stripped of mobile carriers — the **depletion region** — carrying negative charge on the p-side and positive charge on the n-side.

**2. DRIFT — driven by the field those ions create.**

The exposed ions set up an electric field across the depletion region, pointing **from the n-side towards the p-side**. That field sweeps any carrier that enters it:

- **electrons** are swept from the **p-side to the n-side**
- **holes** are swept from the **n-side to the p-side**

**This is a flow of MINORITY carriers** — electrons in p-type material, holes in n-type — and it constitutes the **drift current**, directed from n to p.

**The drift current is OPPOSITE in direction to the diffusion current.** That is the key relationship, and it is what brings the process to a stop.

**Equilibrium.** As diffusion continues, the depletion region widens, the field strengthens and the drift current grows. Diffusion, meanwhile, is slowed by the same field, which now opposes it. **The junction reaches equilibrium when the two currents are equal and opposite**, so the net current is zero.

\(I_{\text{diffusion}} = I_{\text{drift}} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad I_{\text{net}} = 0\)

**What is left behind is the BARRIER POTENTIAL** \(V_0\) — about \(0{\cdot}7\) V for silicon, \(0{\cdot}3\) V for germanium — the potential difference across the depletion region in equilibrium, with the n-side at the higher potential.

**A caution: this potential cannot be measured with a voltmeter** across the diode's terminals, and it cannot drive a current through an external circuit. Connecting leads creates new junctions whose own contact potentials cancel it exactly — as thermodynamics requires, since otherwise a diode alone would be a perpetual source of current.

rows.stem: Draw a labelled ray diagram of an astronomical telescope when final image is formed at infinity. Write the expression for its magnifying power.
rows.solution:
**The ray diagram — astronomical telescope in NORMAL ADJUSTMENT.**

*To draw it:* two converging lenses on a common axis — a large **objective** \(\left(f_o\right)\) on the left and a small **eyepiece** \(\left(f_e\right)\) on the right, separated by \(f_o + f_e\).

**Trace the light in three stages:**

1. **Parallel rays arrive** from a distant object, entering at a small angle \(\alpha\) to the axis. They are parallel because the object is effectively at infinity — that is what "astronomical" means here.
2. The objective brings them to a focus at its **focal plane**, forming a **real, inverted, diminished** image \(A'B'\) of height \(h\). Mark this image at a distance \(f_o\) from the objective.
3. **That image lies exactly at the eyepiece's focus too**, since the lenses are \(f_o + f_e\) apart. The eyepiece therefore sends out a **parallel** beam, and the **final image is at infinity** — inverted, and subtending the larger angle \(\beta\) at the eye.

**Label:** \(f_o\), \(f_e\), the common focal point, the angles \(\alpha\) (at the objective) and \(\beta\) (at the eyepiece), and the eye placed just behind the eyepiece.

**The magnifying power.**

**Angular magnification is the ratio of the angle the image subtends at the eye to the angle the object itself subtends:**

\(m = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}\)

**From the intermediate image of height \(h\)**, using the small-angle approximation at each lens:

\(\alpha \approx \tan\alpha = \dfrac{h}{f_o}, \qquad \beta \approx \tan\beta = \dfrac{h}{f_e}\)

\(m = \dfrac{h/f_e}{h/f_o}\)

\(\boxed{\ m = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}\ }\)

**The height \(h\) cancels**, which is why the answer depends only on the two focal lengths. A minus sign is often carried, \(m = -f_o/f_e\), to record that the image is **inverted** — harmless for astronomy, which is why the correction a terrestrial telescope needs is omitted here.

**The tube length in this adjustment:**

\(L = f_o + f_e\)

**How to make \(m\) large: a LONG objective and a SHORT eyepiece** — the opposite requirement from a microscope, where both must be short. That is why astronomical telescopes are long instruments.

**Why a large objective APERTURE matters just as much.** It does not enter \(m\) at all, but it governs how much light is collected, and the resolving power, which goes as \(\lambda/D\). A large magnification on a small objective yields a big, dim, blurred image — so aperture, not magnification, is the figure of merit quoted for a real telescope.

**Why normal adjustment is preferred.** With the final image at infinity the eye receives parallel light and its ciliary muscle is fully relaxed, so an observer can look for hours without strain. Setting the final image at the near point instead gives slightly more magnification, \(\left(f_o/f_e\right)\left(1 + f_e/D\right)\), at the cost of continuous accommodation.

rows.stem: Define the term 'critical angle'. A small bulb is placed at the bottom of a tank containing a liquid of refractive index \(\mu\) at a depth H. It is observed that the light emerges from a circular area of radius r of the surface. Obtain the expression for r in terms of H and \(\mu\).
rows.solution:
**Definition.**

The **critical angle** is the angle of incidence **in the denser medium** for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is exactly \(90^\circ\) — so the refracted ray grazes along the boundary.

**For angles beyond it, refraction is impossible and the light is TOTALLY INTERNALLY REFLECTED.** Applying Snell's law at that threshold, for a denser medium of refractive index \(\mu\) against air,

\(\mu\sin i_c = 1\times\sin 90^\circ \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \sin i_c = \dfrac{1}{\mu}\)

**The circle of light.**

*The geometry:* the bulb sits at the bottom of the tank at depth \(H\). Rays leave it in all directions and strike the surface at every angle. A ray reaching the surface at an angle **less** than \(i_c\) emerges; one at **more** than \(i_c\) is totally reflected back into the liquid. **The boundary of the bright patch is set by the ray that strikes at exactly \(i_c\)** — which is why the emerging light is confined to a circle rather than covering the whole surface.

**Step 1 — relate \(r\) to \(i_c\) by geometry.** The limiting ray travels from the bulb to the rim of the circle, a horizontal distance \(r\) and a vertical distance \(H\):

\(\tan i_c = \dfrac{r}{H}\)

**Step 2 — express \(\tan i_c\) through \(\mu\).** With \(\sin i_c = 1/\mu\), the adjacent side of the right triangle is \(\sqrt{\mu^{2}-1}\):

\(\cos i_c = \dfrac{\sqrt{\mu^{2}-1}}{\mu}, \qquad \tan i_c = \dfrac{1/\mu}{\sqrt{\mu^{2}-1}/\mu} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu^{2}-1}}\)

**Step 3 — combine.**

\(\dfrac{r}{H} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu^{2}-1}}\)

\(\boxed{\ r = \dfrac{H}{\sqrt{\mu^{2}-1}}\ }\)

*An equivalent route, which avoids the trigonometry:* the limiting ray's own length is \(\sqrt{r^{2}+H^{2}}\), and \(\sin i_c = r/\sqrt{r^{2}+H^{2}} = 1/\mu\). Squaring gives \(\mu^{2}r^{2} = r^{2}+H^{2}\), hence \(\left(\mu^{2}-1\right)r^{2} = H^{2}\) and the same result.

**Reading the answer.** The radius is **proportional to the depth**: a bulb twice as deep lights a circle twice as wide, since the cone of escape has a fixed half-angle \(i_c\). And the radius **shrinks as \(\mu\) grows**, because a denser liquid has a smaller critical angle and a narrower escape cone.

**For water**, \(\mu = 4/3\), so \(\sqrt{\mu^{2}-1} = \sqrt{7}/3 = 0{\cdot}882\) and \(r = 1{\cdot}13\,H\) — a circle a little wider than the depth, and \(i_c = 48{\cdot}6^\circ\).

**The limiting case \(\mu \to 1\)** sends \(r \to \infty\): with no refractive-index step there is no total internal reflection and light escapes everywhere. **And \(\mu\) must exceed \(1\)** for the expression to be real, which is the mathematical statement that total internal reflection needs a denser-to-rarer passage.

**The same geometry seen from above** is why a fish underwater sees the entire sky compressed into a circular window of half-angle \(i_c\) directly overhead — Snell's window — with the surface beyond it acting as a mirror.

rows.stem:
A series combination of circuit elements X and Y is connected across an ac source. It is found that the voltage is ahead of current in phase by \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) radian. When element Y is replaced by element Z, the current leads the voltage by \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) radian.
(a) Identify the elements X, Y and Z.
(b) What will the phase angle and power factor for the circuit be if X, Y and Z were connected in series across the same ac source ? What can you say about the current that flows in the circuit in this case ?
rows.solution:
**(a) Identifying the elements.**

**X appears in BOTH circuits, so it must be the element common to both behaviours** — and since one circuit is inductive and the other capacitive, X can only be the resistor.

**First circuit — voltage LEADS current by \(\pi/4\).** A leading voltage means the circuit is **inductive**. With X as the resistance, Y must supply the inductive reactance.

**Second circuit — current LEADS voltage by \(\pi/4\).** A leading current means **capacitive**. So Z supplies capacitive reactance.

\(\boxed{\ \text{X = RESISTOR}, \qquad \text{Y = INDUCTOR}, \qquad \text{Z = CAPACITOR}\ }\)

**The phase angles also fix the magnitudes**, and this is the part the second half needs.

\(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{X_L}{R} = 1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad X_L = R\)

\(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{X_C}{R} = 1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad X_C = R\)

**So \(X_L = X_C = R\)** — an equality that is not a coincidence but a consequence of both phase angles being the same \(\pi/4\).

**(b) All three in series.**

**The net reactance vanishes:**

\(X = X_L - X_C = R - R = 0\)

**The phase angle:**

\(\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R} = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\ \phi = 0\ }\)

**The power factor:**

\(\boxed{\ \cos\phi = \cos 0 = 1\ }\)

**The current.** With the reactances cancelling, the impedance falls to its smallest possible value:

\(Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + 0} = R\)

\(\boxed{\ I = \dfrac{V}{R}\ \text{— MAXIMUM, and IN PHASE with the voltage}\ }\)

**The circuit is at RESONANCE**, which is the point of the question. \(X_L = X_C\) is exactly the resonance condition, and it was forced by the two equal phase angles rather than by any tuning.

**What resonance means here.** The inductor and capacitor still carry substantial voltages — each equal to \(IR\), since \(X_L = X_C = R\) — but those voltages are \(180^\circ\) apart and **cancel exactly** across the pair. All of the source voltage appears across the resistor.

\(V_L = V_C = IR = V, \qquad V_L + V_C = 0\ \text{(as phasors)}\)

**Energy shuttles between the inductor's magnetic field and the capacitor's electric field**, and the source supplies only what the resistor dissipates. **With \(\cos\phi = 1\) the circuit behaves as if it were purely resistive**, drawing the largest current and delivering the most power it can.

**A note on the frequency.** Resonance holds at one frequency only — \(\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}\) — and here the source's own frequency happens to be it, because \(X_L\) and \(X_C\) were measured as equal at that frequency. Change the source frequency and the balance is lost.

rows.stem: Draw a plot showing the variation of potential energy of a pair of nucleons as a function of their separation (r). Using this plot, show that the nuclear force is (i) attractive for \(r > r_0\), and (ii) repulsive for \(r < r_0\).
rows.solution:
**The plot.**

*To draw it:* potential energy \(U\) in MeV on the vertical axis against the separation \(r\) of the two nucleons, in femtometres, on the horizontal. Mark the axis from \(0\) to about \(3\) fm.

**The shape, which is what the marks are for:**

- At very small \(r\), \(U\) is **large and POSITIVE**, rising almost vertically — reaching \(+100\) MeV and beyond as \(r \to 0\).
- It falls steeply, crossing zero, and reaches a **MINIMUM of about \(-100\) MeV at \(r_0 \approx 0{\cdot}8\) fm**. Label this \(r_0\).
- Beyond \(r_0\) it rises again, more gently, **approaching zero from below** and becoming negligible past about \(2\) to \(3\) fm.

**Mark \(r_0\) on the axis and the value \(U_{\min}\) at the bottom of the well**, since the whole argument refers to them.

**Reading the force from the plot.**

**The force is the negative slope of the potential energy curve:**

\(F = -\dfrac{dU}{dr}\)

**That single relation converts the shape into the answer**, and it is the step the question is testing. A positive \(F\) here means a force pushing the nucleons **apart** (towards increasing \(r\)); a negative \(F\) means a force pulling them **together**.

**(i) For \(r > r_0\) — the force is ATTRACTIVE.**

To the **right** of the minimum the curve **rises** as \(r\) increases, so

\(\dfrac{dU}{dr} > 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad F = -\dfrac{dU}{dr} < 0\)

**A negative force is directed towards decreasing \(r\)** — the nucleons are pulled **together**. That is the attractive nuclear force, and it is what binds a nucleus.

**(ii) For \(r < r_0\) — the force is REPULSIVE.**

To the **left** of the minimum the curve **falls** steeply as \(r\) increases, so

\(\dfrac{dU}{dr} < 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad F = -\dfrac{dU}{dr} > 0\)

**A positive force is directed towards increasing \(r\)** — the nucleons are pushed **apart**. The nuclear force turns strongly repulsive at very short range.

**At \(r = r_0\) exactly**, the curve is flat, \(dU/dr = 0\) and \(F = 0\). **This is the equilibrium separation**, and it is a **stable** one because the potential is a minimum: displace the pair either way and the force pushes it back.

**Why the repulsive core matters.** Without it, nucleons would collapse together and every nucleus would have the same tiny size. The hard core sets a minimum spacing, which is why **nuclear density is nearly the same for all nuclei** and why the nuclear radius follows \(R = R_0A^{1/3}\) — each added nucleon takes up its own fixed volume.

**Why the attraction dies away so fast.** The nuclear force is **short-ranged**, effectively zero beyond about \(3\) fm — quite unlike the Coulomb force, which reaches across the whole nucleus. A nucleon therefore attracts only its immediate neighbours, and that **saturation** is what flattens the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve across the middle of the periodic table.

**A note on the depth.** The well is around \(100\) MeV deep, while a nucleon's binding energy is only about \(8\) MeV. The difference is the nucleon's kinetic energy inside the nucleus — it sits well up inside the well rather than at the bottom of it.
